sectionTitle: Reactions of alkenes and alcohols (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with a double carbon-carbon bond. The general formula for the homologous series of alkenes is Cₙ H₂ₙ
Alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
The first four members of the homologous series of alkenes are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
Alkene molecules can be represented in the following forms:
C₃ H₆
or
Students do not need to know the names of individual alkenes other than ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
Alkenes are hydrocarbons with the functional group C=C.
It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determine the reactions of organic compounds.
Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions in the same way as other hydrocarbons, but they tend to burn in air with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion.
Alkenes react with hydrogen, water and the halogens, by the addition of atoms across the carbon-carbon double bond so that the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond.
Students should be able to:
describe the reactions and conditions for the addition of hydrogen, water and halogens to alkenes
draw fully displayed structural formulae of the first four members of the alkenes and the products of their addition reactions with hydrogen, water, chlorine, bromine and iodine.
Alcohols contain the functional group –OH.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol are the first four members of a homologous series of alcohols.
Alcohols can be represented in the following forms:
CH₃ CH₂ OH
or
Students should be able to:
describe what happens when any of the first four alcohols react with sodium, burn in air, are added to water, react with an oxidising agent
recall the main uses of these alcohols.
Aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.
Students should know the conditions used for fermentation of sugar using yeast.
Students should be able to recognise alcohols from their names or from given formulae.
Students do not need to know the names of individual alcohols other than methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol.
Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of alcohols other than for combustion reactions.
Carboxylic acids have the functional group –COOH.
The first four members of a homologous series of carboxylic acids are methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
The structures of carboxylic acids can be represented in the following forms:
CH₃ COOH
or
Students should be able to:
describe what happens when any of the first four carboxylic acids react with carbonates, dissolve in water, react with alcohols
(HT only) explain why carboxylic acids are weak acids in terms of ionisation and pH (see Strong and weak acids (HT only) ).
Students should be able to recognise carboxylic acids from their names or from given formulae.
Students do not need to know the names of individual carboxylic acids other than methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of carboxylic acids.
Students do not need to know the names of esters other than ethyl ethanoate.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual alkenes other than ethene, propene, butene and pentene.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only ethene, propene, butene and pentene are named anywhere in this material. No alkene beyond pentene is required by any question. Invented or later names such as methene and hexene appear only as wrong options in the one list question, where the point is that they do not belong; nothing asks a student to recall a name, a formula or a reaction beyond the four. General points about the series are made through the general formula CₙH₂ₙ or through one of the four named members. Positional names such as but-1-ene, and the idea that a double bond can sit in different places along a chain, are not introduced.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual alcohols other than methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every alcohol a student is asked to know or work with here is methanol, ethanol, propanol or butanol. Recognition questions work from the –OH group or from those four names. Pentanol appears only inside wrong options in the one list question, where the point is that it falls outside the required four; no question asks for its formula, properties or reactions. Names such as propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, and branched alcohols, are not used.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of alcohols other than for combustion reactions.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The only balanced equation asked for anywhere in this material is the complete combustion of ethanol, C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O. The reactions of alcohols with sodium, with water and with an oxidising agent are handled in words and by naming products only; no question asks for, or offers as an option, an equation for those reactions, and sodium ethoxide is never named.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of individual carboxylic acids other than methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid are named. Pentanoic acid appears only inside wrong options in the one list question, where the point is that it lies outside the required four; no question asks for its formula or its reactions. Recognition is tested from the –COOH group and from the -oic acid ending, not from names beyond these four.

scopeNotes.statement: Students are not expected to write balanced chemical equations for the reactions of carboxylic acids.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: No equation for a reaction of a carboxylic acid appears in this material, in a question stem, an option or a correction. Reactions with carbonates, with water and with alcohols are described in words and by naming the products, and the ionisation of a weak acid is described qualitatively as partial rather than through an equilibrium equation.

scopeNotes.statement: Students do not need to know the names of esters other than ethyl ethanoate.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Ethyl ethanoate is the only ester named anywhere here, and it appears only as the product of ethanoic acid with ethanol. Where an ester formula is used as a distractor it is that of ethyl ethanoate, CH₃COOCH₂CH₃. No other ester is named, and no question asks a student to name an ester from an acid and an alcohol.

concepts.definition: A hydrocarbon with a double carbon-carbon bond. It contains carbon and hydrogen only; the C=C is what separates it from an alkane.
CₙH₂ₙ. Every member has twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms: C₂H₄, C₃H₆, C₄H₈, C₅H₁₀. The alkanes, by contrast, are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂.
Describes a molecule with a carbon-carbon double bond. An alkene is unsaturated because it contains two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.
Describes a molecule in which every carbon-carbon bond is single, so each carbon atom is joined to as many atoms as it can be. The alkanes are saturated.
Ethene (C₂H₄), propene (C₃H₆), butene (C₄H₈) and pentene (C₅H₁₀). The series begins at two carbon atoms because a C=C needs two carbon atoms.
A formula such as C₃H₆ that gives the number of atoms of each element in one molecule. It does not show how the atoms are joined or where the double bond lies.
A drawing showing every atom and every bond in the molecule, so a C=C appears as two lines between two carbon atoms. It carries more information than a molecular formula.
The group of atoms in a molecule that gives a homologous series its characteristic reactions. Members of a series share a functional group and so react in the same ways.
The carbon-carbon double bond, the functional group of the alkenes. It is the site of their addition reactions.
It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds, so ethene, propene, butene and pentene all react in the same ways.
Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions like other hydrocarbons, but tend to burn in air with smoky flames because combustion is incomplete and carbon is released as soot.
A reaction in which atoms add across the carbon-carbon double bond so that the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond. Alkenes react in this way with hydrogen, water and the halogens.
Hydrogen adds across the C=C over a nickel catalyst at about 150 °C, turning the alkene into the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms: ethene gives ethane.
Ethene reacts with steam in the presence of a catalyst, at high temperature and pressure, and water adds across the double bond to give an alcohol: ethene gives ethanol.
Chlorine, bromine or iodine adds across the C=C at room temperature. Bromine water is decolourised, which is the test that tells an alkene from an alkane.
A compound containing the functional group –OH. Alcohols are not hydrocarbons, because they contain oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen.
Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol, the first four members of a homologous series of alcohols.
Ethanol may be written as CH₃CH₂OH, which shows the –OH group and how the carbon atoms are grouped, or drawn as a displayed formula showing every bond.
Sodium reacts with an alcohol, fizzing steadily and releasing hydrogen gas. The reaction is gentler than that of sodium with water.
Alcohols burn in air. Complete combustion gives carbon dioxide and water, for example C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.
The first four alcohols dissolve in water, and the solutions formed have a neutral pH.
Warming an alcohol with an oxidising agent produces the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms: ethanol gives ethanoic acid.
The first four alcohols are used as fuels and as solvents; ethanol is also the alcohol in alcoholic drinks.
The process in which aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.
Yeast is added to an aqueous sugar solution kept warm at about 30 °C with air kept out. Too high a temperature kills the yeast and stops the process.
An alcohol can be picked out from a name ending in -ol, such as butanol, or from a formula containing the –OH group, such as CH₃CH₂OH.
A compound containing the functional group –COOH. Its aqueous solutions are acidic.
Methanoic acid, ethanoic acid, propanoic acid and butanoic acid, the first four members of a homologous series of carboxylic acids.
Ethanoic acid may be written as CH₃COOH, which shows the carboxyl group joined to a CH₃ group, or drawn as a displayed formula showing every bond.
The drawing shows the C=O and the O–H of the carboxyl group as separate bonds, which CH₃COOH written on one line does not set out.
A carboxylic acid reacts with a carbonate, fizzing as carbon dioxide is given off, in the same way as other acids do.
Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to give acidic solutions with a pH below 7.
A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol, in the presence of an acid catalyst, to produce an ester. Ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate.
An acid that is only partially ionised in aqueous solution. The carboxylic acids are weak acids.
Because only some molecules ionise, a weak acid solution has a lower concentration of H+ ions, and so a higher pH, than a strong acid of the same concentration.
A carboxylic acid can be picked out from a name ending in -oic acid, such as propanoic acid, or from a formula containing –COOH, such as CH₃COOH.

misconceptions.question: What is the general formula of the alkenes?
misconceptions.correct: CₙH₂ₙ: propene is C₃H₆ and butene is C₄H₈.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkenes have the general formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂, the same as the alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The alkanes are met first and their formula is drilled hard, so CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ becomes the formula reached for whenever a hydrocarbon series is named.
misconceptions.correction: The two series differ. Alkanes are CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ and alkenes are CₙH₂ₙ. Checking a known member settles it: propene is C₃H₆, which is 2 × 3 hydrogen atoms, not 2 × 3 + 2.

misconceptions.question: Propane is C₃H₈. How many hydrogen atoms are in propene?
misconceptions.correct: Six, because propene is C₃H₆.
misconceptions.misconception: An unsaturated molecule holds more hydrogen atoms than the saturated one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday use 'saturated' means soaked or full, so students expect the unsaturated molecule to take on extra hydrogen rather than to have less of it.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states it directly: alkene molecules are unsaturated because they contain two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

misconceptions.question: Which alkene is the first member of the series?
misconceptions.correct: Ethene, with two carbon atoms.
misconceptions.misconception: The series begins with a one-carbon member, 'methene', or begins at propene.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The alkanes begin with methane, so students expect every homologous series to start at one carbon atom and pattern-match the prefixes.
misconceptions.correction: A carbon-carbon double bond needs two carbon atoms, so the alkenes begin at ethene. The four named members are ethene, propene, butene and pentene.

misconceptions.question: What does a molecular formula such as C₃H₆ show?
misconceptions.correct: How many atoms of each element are in one molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: A molecular formula also shows where the double bond is and how the atoms are joined.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae and drawings are used side by side in lessons, so students stop distinguishing what each representation actually carries.
misconceptions.correction: C₃H₆ counts atoms only. To see the bonds, and where the C=C lies, a fully displayed formula is needed.

misconceptions.question: Does the double bond make an alkene unreactive?
misconceptions.correct: No: the C=C is the reactive part, and it is where addition happens.
misconceptions.misconception: A double bond is stronger, so alkenes are less reactive than alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that two bonds take more energy to break than one, and conclude the molecule must be harder to react.
misconceptions.correction: Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes. The double bond is a site where atoms can add on, which is why bromine water is decolourised by an alkene but not by an alkane.

misconceptions.question: Why do ethene, propene and butene react in the same ways?
misconceptions.correct: Because they share the same functional group, C=C.
misconceptions.misconception: Each compound has its own reactions that must be learned separately.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Reactions are often met one equation at a time, so the pattern behind them is missed and chemistry looks like a list to memorise.
misconceptions.correction: It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds; every member of a series reacts in the same ways.

misconceptions.question: How do alkenes tend to burn in air?
misconceptions.correct: With smoky flames, because combustion is incomplete.
misconceptions.misconception: Alkenes burn with clean blue flames because hydrocarbons burn completely in air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The Bunsen burner burning methane with a clean blue flame is the image students carry, and it is applied to every hydrocarbon.
misconceptions.correction: Alkenes have a higher proportion of carbon, so in air the oxygen supply is not enough to burn all of it. Combustion is incomplete and the flame is smoky.

misconceptions.question: What happens to an alkene molecule in an addition reaction?
misconceptions.correct: Atoms add across the C=C, which becomes a single bond.
misconceptions.misconception: The molecule breaks apart at the double bond into two smaller molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'The double bond breaks' is a phrase used in class, and students take it to mean the carbon chain itself splits, as it does in cracking.
misconceptions.correction: Only one of the two bonds between the carbon atoms is used. The carbon chain stays whole and the double bond becomes a single carbon-carbon bond.

misconceptions.question: How does bromine react with ethene?
misconceptions.correct: By addition, giving C₂H₄Br₂ with no other product.
misconceptions.misconception: Bromine replaces a hydrogen atom, giving C₂H₃Br and hydrogen bromide.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Substitution is met first, with alkanes and halogens in ultraviolet light, and the pattern is carried over to the alkenes.
misconceptions.correction: Alkanes substitute, alkenes add. The double bond opens and both halogen atoms join the molecule, so nothing is left over.

misconceptions.question: What conditions are needed to add hydrogen to an alkene?
misconceptions.correct: A nickel catalyst at about 150 °C.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet light is needed, as in the reactions of alkanes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ultraviolet light is the one condition students remember from organic chemistry, so it is offered for any organic reaction.
misconceptions.correction: Ultraviolet light belongs to the substitution reactions of alkanes. Hydrogenation of an alkene uses a nickel catalyst at roughly 150 °C.

misconceptions.question: What is made when ethene reacts with steam?
misconceptions.correct: Ethanol, because water adds across the double bond.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethane is made, or the ethene simply dissolves in the water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydrogen and water both add across a C=C, so their products are mixed up, and 'steam' is read as a solvent rather than a reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Adding hydrogen gives the alkane; adding water gives the alcohol. Ethene with steam and a catalyst gives ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH.

misconceptions.question: What does a fully displayed formula add to CH₃CH₂OH or C₃H₆?
misconceptions.correct: It shows every atom and every bond in the molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: The drawing carries no more information than the written formula.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both forms describe the same molecule, so students conclude they say the same thing and treat the drawing as decoration.
misconceptions.correction: The written forms count or group the atoms; the displayed formula shows the bonds, so a double bond or an O–H bond can be seen directly.

misconceptions.question: Is an alcohol a hydrocarbon?
misconceptions.correct: No: it contains oxygen as well as carbon and hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Alcohols are hydrocarbons, like the alkanes and the alkenes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Alcohols are taught in the same topic as alkanes and alkenes and their names look similar, so the oxygen atom is overlooked.
misconceptions.correction: A hydrocarbon contains only hydrogen and carbon. Ethanol is CH₃CH₂OH, so it holds an oxygen atom and cannot be a hydrocarbon.

misconceptions.question: Are alcohol solutions alkaline?
misconceptions.correct: No: the first four alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions.
misconceptions.misconception: The –OH group makes alcohols alkaline, because alkalis contain OH.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Hydroxide ions, OH-, are met in alkalis, and the same two letters in the alcohol functional group are read as the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: In an alcohol the –OH is covalently bonded within the molecule and no hydroxide ions are released, so the solution is neutral.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when sodium is added to ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: Hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxygen is given off, because the alcohol contains an oxygen atom.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students look for the released gas among the atoms they can see, and the O of the –OH group is the obvious candidate.
misconceptions.correction: It is the hydrogen of the –OH group that is displaced by sodium, so hydrogen gas fizzes off, just as when sodium reacts with water.

misconceptions.question: What are the products of the complete combustion of ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen gas is a product, or carbon monoxide forms even in plenty of air.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The hydrogen atoms in the formula are tracked as though they leave unchanged, and incomplete combustion is applied whatever the air supply.
misconceptions.correction: In complete combustion every carbon atom ends up in CO₂ and every hydrogen atom in H₂O: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O.

misconceptions.question: What is the pH of an aqueous solution of ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: Neutral, about pH 7.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethanol solutions are acidic, because ethanol is related to ethanoic acid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The names ethanol and ethanoic acid are almost the same, and both molecules contain an O–H, so their solutions are expected to behave alike.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions. Only after oxidation, when the carboxyl group has formed, is the solution acidic.

misconceptions.question: What is formed when ethanol is warmed with an oxidising agent?
misconceptions.correct: Ethanoic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Ethene is formed, or the ethanol is burned to carbon dioxide and water.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Several reactions of ethanol are met close together, and 'oxidising agent' is read as another way of saying burning, or confused with dehydration.
misconceptions.correction: Oxidation of an alcohol gives the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms, so ethanol gives ethanoic acid.

misconceptions.question: At what temperature is sugar solution fermented?
misconceptions.correct: At about 30 °C.
misconceptions.misconception: A high temperature such as 100 °C is used, to make the reaction go faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rate work teaches that heating speeds reactions up, and the rule is applied without asking what heat does to the yeast.
misconceptions.correction: Yeast is a living organism and its enzymes are denatured by heat, so fermentation is carried out warm, at roughly 30 °C, not hot.

misconceptions.question: Is air needed for fermentation?
misconceptions.correct: No: fermentation is carried out with air kept out.
misconceptions.misconception: Air must be bubbled through, because yeast needs oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Respiration is remembered as needing oxygen, so oxygen is assumed to be needed here too.
misconceptions.correction: Fermentation is anaerobic. If air is present the ethanol is oxidised, so the vessel is kept sealed from the air.

misconceptions.question: How can you tell an alcohol from a carboxylic acid by name?
misconceptions.correct: Alcohols end in -ol; carboxylic acids end in -oic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Names such as propanol and propanoic acid describe the same kind of compound.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two endings differ by very little in print and the stems are identical, so the families blur together.
misconceptions.correction: The ending names the functional group. Propanol contains –OH; propanoic acid contains –COOH and gives an acidic solution.

misconceptions.question: Does a weak acid ionise completely in water?
misconceptions.correct: No: only some of its molecules ionise.
misconceptions.misconception: All acids ionise completely in aqueous solution.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Strong acids are met first and their full ionisation is taken as what 'acid' means.
misconceptions.correction: A strong acid is completely ionised in solution; a weak acid, such as a carboxylic acid, is only partially ionised.

misconceptions.question: Which gas is given off when ethanoic acid is added to a carbonate?
misconceptions.correct: Carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Hydrogen is given off, as when an acid reacts with a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two fizzing reactions are learned close together and the gases are swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Acid with a metal gives hydrogen; acid with a carbonate gives carbon dioxide, which turns limewater cloudy.

misconceptions.question: What is formed when a carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol?
misconceptions.correct: An ester, together with water.
misconceptions.misconception: A salt and water are formed, as in a neutralisation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Acid plus something gives a salt and water' is a strong rule from acid chemistry, and the alcohol is treated as if it were an alkali.
misconceptions.correction: An alcohol is not an alkali. The acid and the alcohol join to make an ester: ethanoic acid with ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate.

misconceptions.question: What does calling ethanoic acid a weak acid mean?
misconceptions.correct: That it is only partially ionised in solution.
misconceptions.misconception: That the solution is dilute, or that it does not react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech weak and dilute mean much the same, and 'weak' sounds like 'unable'.
misconceptions.correction: Strength is about the fraction of molecules that ionise; concentration is about how much acid is dissolved. A weak acid still reacts, for instance with carbonates.

misconceptions.question: How does the pH of ethanoic acid compare with hydrochloric acid at the same concentration?
misconceptions.correct: The ethanoic acid has the higher pH.
misconceptions.misconception: Both have the same pH, or the ethanoic acid has the lower one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Equal concentrations are assumed to mean equal numbers of H+ ions, and the difference between strength and concentration is not applied.
misconceptions.correction: Only some ethanoic acid molecules ionise, so its solution has fewer H+ ions and a higher pH than hydrochloric acid of the same concentration.

misconceptions.question: Is CH₃COOH an alcohol, since it contains an O–H?
misconceptions.correct: No: the –COOH group makes it a carboxylic acid.
misconceptions.misconception: Any formula containing OH is an alcohol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students scan for the letters OH rather than reading the whole functional group.
misconceptions.correction: In a carboxylic acid the O–H sits on a carbon that is also double bonded to oxygen. That whole –COOH group, not the O–H alone, is the functional group.

misconceptions.question: Which bonds are found in a saturated molecule?
misconceptions.correct: Single carbon-carbon bonds only.
misconceptions.misconception: Saturated and unsaturated are used the other way round, so an alkene is called saturated.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The two terms are abstract, sound similar and are introduced together, so they are easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: Saturated means every carbon-carbon bond is single, as in the alkanes. Unsaturated means a C=C is present, as in the alkenes.

misconceptions.question: Why do alkenes burn with smoky flames?
misconceptions.correct: Because combustion is incomplete and carbon is released.
misconceptions.misconception: Because there is too much oxygen present when they burn.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Smoke is linked with something being wrong with the air supply, but the direction of the effect is guessed.
misconceptions.correction: A smoky flame means too little oxygen for the carbon present, so some carbon is not oxidised and appears as soot.

misconceptions.question: Does the product of an addition reaction still contain a C=C?
misconceptions.correct: No: the double bond becomes a single bond.
misconceptions.misconception: The double bond survives, with the new atoms joined on elsewhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The extra atoms are pictured as being tacked onto the ends of the molecule, leaving the middle untouched.
misconceptions.correction: The atoms add across the double bond itself, so in the product the two carbon atoms are joined by a single bond.

misconceptions.question: What does a molecular formula such as C₂H₆O give?
misconceptions.correct: The number of atoms of each element in a molecule.
misconceptions.misconception: It gives only the ratio of the atoms, or is written straight into an equation without balancing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Empirical formulae and molecular formulae are met together, and equation writing is treated as translation rather than as balancing.
misconceptions.correction: A molecular formula gives real numbers, not a ratio, and an equation is only correct when the atoms of each element balance on both sides.

misconceptions.question: Does sodium react with ethanol?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: it fizzes and releases hydrogen.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium reacts only with water, so nothing happens with an alcohol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The reaction of sodium with water is memorable and is taken to be the only reaction sodium has with an O–H containing liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Alcohols react with sodium in the same way as water, though more gently, giving off hydrogen gas.

misconceptions.question: Do ethanol and ethanoic acid dissolve in water?
misconceptions.correct: Yes: both are soluble in water.
misconceptions.misconception: Organic liquids do not mix with water; they float as a separate layer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Oil and water is the everyday example of an organic liquid meeting water, and it is generalised.
misconceptions.correction: The first four alcohols dissolve to give neutral solutions and the carboxylic acids dissolve to give acidic solutions.

misconceptions.question: How many hydrogen atoms are added when hydrogen reacts with propene?
misconceptions.correct: Two, giving propane, C₃H₈.
misconceptions.misconception: One hydrogen atom is added, or two whole molecules of hydrogen are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students count the molecule H₂ as a single unit of one atom, or add reagent until the formula looks familiar.
misconceptions.correction: One molecule of H₂ supplies two atoms, one to each carbon of the double bond, so C₃H₆ becomes C₃H₈.

misconceptions.question: What are the main uses of the first four alcohols?
misconceptions.correct: As fuels and as solvents.
misconceptions.misconception: Alcohols are only used in alcoholic drinks.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word alcohol has an everyday meaning that crowds out the chemistry.
misconceptions.correction: Methanol and ethanol burn cleanly and are used as fuels, and alcohols dissolve substances that water will not, so they are widely used as solvents.

mcqs.stem: What is the general formula for the homologous series of alkenes?

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ — twice as many hydrogen atoms as carbon atoms
options.rationale: The specification gives CₙH₂ₙ for the alkenes: propene is C₃H₆ and butene is C₄H₈.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ — two hydrogen atoms more than twice the carbon
options.rationale: The general formula of the alkanes, learned first and then applied to any hydrocarbon series.

options.text: CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ — two hydrogen atoms fewer than twice the carbons
options.rationale: Takes 'two fewer hydrogen atoms' and subtracts them from 2n rather than from the alkane's 2n + 2.

options.text: CₙHₙ — one hydrogen atom for every carbon atom present
options.rationale: Assumes a double bond leaves room for only one hydrogen atom on each carbon atom.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is a correct description of an alkene?

options.text: A hydrocarbon in which every carbon bond is a single bond
options.rationale: This describes an alkane; chosen by students who have not separated the two series.

options.text: A hydrocarbon containing a carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: Alkenes are hydrocarbons with a double carbon-carbon bond, as the specification states.

options.text: A compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen atoms
options.rationale: Confuses an alkene with an alcohol; a hydrocarbon contains no oxygen at all.

options.text: A hydrocarbon made unreactive by its double bond
options.rationale: Reads a double bond as extra strength, so the molecule is assumed to be hard to react.

mcqs.stem: Propane has the formula C₃H₈. What is the formula of propene?

options.text: C₃H₁₀, which is two hydrogen atoms more than propane
options.rationale: Comes from thinking 'unsaturated' means the molecule holds extra hydrogen atoms.

options.text: C₃H₆, two hydrogen atoms fewer than propane
options.rationale: An alkene has two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: C₃H₈, exactly the same formula as propane has
options.rationale: Assumes the alkane and the alkene differ only in name, not in the number of atoms.

options.text: C₃H₇, one hydrogen atom fewer than propane has
options.rationale: Removes a single hydrogen atom rather than the pair lost when a double bond forms.

mcqs.stem: Why is propene described as unsaturated?

options.text: It has two hydrogen atoms fewer than propane does
options.rationale: The specification defines unsaturated in exactly this way: two fewer hydrogen atoms than the alkane with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: It has two hydrogen atoms more than propane does
options.rationale: 'Unsaturated' is read as 'has room for more', and the atom count is then moved the wrong way.

options.text: Every bond between its carbon atoms is a single bond
options.rationale: Swaps the meanings of saturated and unsaturated; single bonds throughout describe an alkane.

options.text: Each carbon atom is joined to as many atoms as it can be
options.rationale: This is the description of a saturated molecule, offered as though it meant unsaturated.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alkenes?

options.text: Methene, ethene, propene and pentene
options.rationale: Assumes the alkenes start at one carbon atom, as the alkanes do with methane.

options.text: Ethene, ethane, butene and butane
options.rationale: Mixes alkanes into the alkene series, which happens when the -ane and -ene endings are not held apart.

options.text: Ethene, propene, butene and pentene
options.rationale: These are the four members named in the specification.

options.text: Ethene, propene, butene and hexene
options.rationale: Skips pentene, usually because the series is recalled by counting carbon atoms carelessly.

mcqs.stem: What does the molecular formula C₃H₆ tell you about a propene molecule?

options.text: The number of atoms of each element in the molecule
options.rationale: A molecular formula gives the actual count of each kind of atom: three carbon and six hydrogen.

options.text: Where the double bond lies and how the atoms join
options.rationale: Expects a molecular formula to carry structural detail that only a displayed formula shows.

options.text: Only the ratio of carbon to hydrogen atoms present
options.rationale: Confuses the molecular formula with a simplest ratio; C₃H₆ gives real numbers, not just 1:2.

options.text: Every bond in the molecule, shown drawn out
options.rationale: Treats a molecular formula and a displayed formula as carrying the same information.

mcqs.stem: Which of these formulae fits the general formula CₙH₂ₙ?

options.text: C₄H₁₀
options.rationale: An alkane, CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; picked when the hydrogen count is not checked against the carbon count.

options.text: C₂H₅OH
options.rationale: An alcohol, and not a hydrocarbon at all, but it is often read as just another carbon compound.

options.text: CH₃COOH
options.rationale: A carboxylic acid; chosen when a formula is scanned for carbon and hydrogen without counting.

options.text: C₃H₆
options.rationale: Six hydrogen atoms for three carbon atoms is 2n hydrogen atoms, so this fits the alkenes.

mcqs.stem: Propene can also be drawn as a fully displayed formula. What does that show that C₃H₆ does not?

options.text: Nothing new; the same information is drawn out
options.rationale: Assumes a drawing is decoration rather than a different level of information.

options.text: Only how many atoms of each element are present
options.rationale: That is what the molecular formula already gives, so it cannot be what the drawing adds.

options.text: Every atom and every bond, including the double bond
options.rationale: A displayed formula sets out each bond, so the position of the C=C can be seen.

options.text: How the molecules are arranged in a sample of propene
options.rationale: Confuses the structure of one molecule with the arrangement of many molecules in a substance.

mcqs.stem: What is the functional group of the alkenes?

options.text: The –OH group found in alcohols
options.rationale: The functional group of the alcohols, mixed up when the families are learned together.

options.text: The –COOH group of the acids
options.rationale: The functional group of the carboxylic acids, offered when group and family are not linked.

options.text: The carbon–carbon double bond, C=C
options.rationale: The specification gives the functional group of the alkenes as C=C.

options.text: A single carbon–carbon bond, C–C
options.rationale: Chosen by students who have not registered that it is the double bond that defines an alkene.

mcqs.stem: Ethene, propene and butene all decolourise bromine water. What best explains this?

options.text: They share a functional group, so they react alike
options.rationale: It is the generality of reactions of functional groups that determines the reactions of organic compounds.

options.text: Each one has its own reaction and the likeness is chance
options.rationale: Treats every compound as a separate case to be memorised rather than as a member of a family.

options.text: They all contain the same number of carbon atoms
options.rationale: Simply untrue: ethene, propene and butene have two, three and four carbon atoms.

options.text: They are all gases, so they mix easily with bromine
options.rationale: Puts the explanation in the physical state instead of in the C=C group that reacts.

mcqs.stem: How do alkenes tend to burn in air?

options.text: With clean blue flames, because combustion is complete
options.rationale: Assumes any hydrocarbon burning in air burns cleanly, as methane does in a lit Bunsen.

options.text: They do not burn at all, as the double bond is stable
options.rationale: Reads a double bond as making the molecule unreactive, so combustion is ruled out.

options.text: With smoky flames, because combustion is incomplete
options.rationale: The specification states that alkenes tend to burn in air with smoky flames because of incomplete combustion.

options.text: With smoky flames, because the oxygen supply is too great
options.rationale: Has the cause the wrong way round; smokiness comes from too little oxygen for the carbon present.

mcqs.stem: Ethene is burned in plenty of air. What are the products of complete combustion?

options.text: Carbon dioxide and soot
options.rationale: Describes incomplete combustion, which is what happens in a limited air supply, not in plenty of air.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: Assumes the hydrogen in the molecule is released as a gas rather than ending up in water.

options.text: Carbon monoxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: Tracks the hydrogen atoms out as a gas and leaves the carbon only half oxidised, though air is in excess.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.rationale: Alkenes react with oxygen in combustion reactions in the same way as other hydrocarbons.

mcqs.stem: Hydrogen adds to ethene. What happens to the carbon–carbon double bond?

options.text: It stays a double bond in the product
options.rationale: Pictures the hydrogen simply joining on somewhere without the double bond being used up.

options.text: It breaks and the molecule splits into two
options.rationale: Reads 'the double bond breaks' as the whole carbon chain breaking apart.

options.text: It is swapped for a bond to a hydrogen atom
options.rationale: Applies the substitution pattern met with alkanes to a reaction that is an addition.

options.text: It becomes a single carbon–carbon bond
options.rationale: In addition reactions atoms add across the double bond so that it becomes a single carbon-carbon bond.

mcqs.stem: Which set of substances react with alkenes by addition across the double bond?

options.text: Hydrogen, water and the halogens
options.rationale: The specification lists hydrogen, water and the halogens as adding across the carbon-carbon double bond.

options.text: Oxygen, carbon dioxide and nitrogen
options.rationale: Brings combustion into a question about addition, so oxygen is assumed to add across the bond.

options.text: Oxygen, sodium and the halogens
options.rationale: Borrows sodium from the reactions of the alcohols, which is a different family.

options.text: Sodium, oxygen and carbonates
options.rationale: Mixes in reagents met with the carboxylic acids rather than with the alkenes.

mcqs.stem: What conditions are used for the addition of hydrogen to an alkene?

options.text: Ultraviolet light, no catalyst
options.rationale: Takes the conditions for the substitution reaction of alkanes with halogens.

options.text: Steam with a catalyst at 300 °C
options.rationale: These are the conditions for adding water, not hydrogen, to an alkene.

options.text: Yeast at about 30 °C with no air
options.rationale: Fermentation conditions, recalled because they are the other set of numbers in this topic.

options.text: A nickel catalyst at about 150 °C
options.rationale: Hydrogenation of an alkene is carried out over a nickel catalyst at roughly 150 °C.

mcqs.stem: Ethene is reacted with steam in the presence of a catalyst. What is produced?

options.text: Ethane gas, an alkane, C₂H₆
options.rationale: Confuses adding water with adding hydrogen, so the alkane is given as the product.

options.text: Ethanol, an alcohol, CH₃CH₂OH
options.rationale: Water adds across the double bond, so the product of hydrating ethene is ethanol.

options.text: Ethanoic acid, an acid, CH₃COOH
options.rationale: Jumps to the oxidation product, skipping the alcohol that is actually formed.

options.text: A solution of ethene in hot water
options.rationale: Treats the steam as a solvent rather than as a reactant that adds across the C=C.

mcqs.stem: Bromine water is shaken with ethene. What is seen, and what is formed?

options.text: The orange colour goes as C₂H₃Br and HBr form
options.rationale: Right observation, wrong mechanism: this is substitution, which is how alkanes react.

options.text: The orange colour stays, as ethene is saturated
options.rationale: Calls the alkene saturated, so the test that distinguishes it from an alkane is reversed.

options.text: The orange colour deepens as bromine adds on
options.rationale: Assumes adding bromine into a molecule must make the mixture more strongly coloured.

options.text: The orange colour goes and C₂H₄Br₂ forms
options.rationale: Bromine adds across the double bond, so the bromine colour is lost and a dibromo compound forms.

mcqs.stem: Ethene reacts with chlorine. Which describes the product?

options.text: C₂H₃Cl, with a hydrogen atom replaced by chlorine
options.rationale: The substitution product; chosen by students applying the alkane reaction to an alkene.

options.text: C₂H₄ and Cl₂ are unchanged, as there is no reaction
options.rationale: Assumes the double bond makes ethene unreactive towards chlorine.

options.text: C₂H₄Cl₂, one chlorine atom on each carbon atom
options.rationale: Both chlorine atoms add across the double bond, giving a saturated molecule with two chlorine atoms.

options.text: C₂H₄Cl₂, still holding a carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: Right formula, wrong structure: the double bond has been used in forming the two new bonds.

mcqs.stem: Propene reacts with hydrogen. How many hydrogen atoms are in the displayed formula of the product?

options.text: Six, as propene already has six of them
options.rationale: Leaves the alkene unchanged, which follows from thinking the double bond survives.

options.text: Seven, one hydrogen atom having added on
options.rationale: Adds a single hydrogen atom instead of the pair that a molecule of H₂ supplies.

options.text: Eight, since the product is propane, C₃H₈
options.rationale: Two hydrogen atoms add across the double bond of C₃H₆, giving C₃H₈.

options.text: Ten, since two molecules of H₂ add on
options.rationale: Adds H₂ twice, which the single double bond cannot accommodate.

mcqs.stem: Which functional group is found in every alcohol?

options.text: The carboxyl group, –COOH
options.rationale: The carboxylic acid group; the two families are confused because both contain O and H.

options.text: The hydroxyl group, –OH
options.rationale: The specification states that alcohols contain the functional group -OH.

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: The alkene functional group, chosen when alcohols are still thought of as hydrocarbons.

options.text: The hydroxide ion, OH⁻
options.rationale: Reads the covalently bonded –OH group as the ion found in alkalis.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of alcohols?

options.text: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and pentanol
options.rationale: Drops butanol and puts the fifth member in its place, from counting along the series carelessly.

options.text: Ethanol, propanol, butanol, pentanol
options.rationale: Starts the alcohols at two carbon atoms, as the alkenes start at ethene, and adds a fifth member.

options.text: Methane, ethanol, propanol and butanol
options.rationale: Writes the alkane methane where methanol belongs, so the -ol ending that marks an alcohol is lost.

options.text: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol
options.rationale: These are the four alcohols named in the specification.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol can be represented as CH₃CH₂OH. What does this form show?

options.text: Only the total number of atoms of each element
options.rationale: That is what C₂H₆O gives; this form carries more than a simple atom count.

options.text: The –OH group and how the carbon atoms are grouped
options.rationale: This form sets out the groups in the molecule, so the functional group can be picked out.

options.text: Every bond in the molecule, drawn in full
options.rationale: Confuses this written form with a fully displayed formula.

options.text: That ethanol releases hydroxide ions in water
options.rationale: Reads the –OH group as a separate ion, which would make ethanol an alkali.

mcqs.stem: A displayed formula of ethanol is drawn instead of writing CH₃CH₂OH. What does the drawing add?

options.text: It shows nothing new about the ethanol molecule
options.rationale: Assumes the two representations are interchangeable in the information they carry.

options.text: It shows every bond, including the O–H bond
options.rationale: A displayed formula shows all of the bonds in the molecule, which the written form does not.

options.text: It shows how many molecules are in the sample
options.rationale: Confuses the structure of one molecule with the amount of substance.

options.text: It shows the charge on each atom present
options.rationale: Expects charges because the –OH group is being read as an ion.

mcqs.stem: A small piece of sodium is added to ethanol. What is observed?

options.text: It fizzes steadily and hydrogen gas is given off
options.rationale: Alcohols react with sodium to give off hydrogen, more gently than water does.

options.text: It fizzes gently and oxygen is given off
options.rationale: Sees oxygen in the –OH group and assumes that is the gas released.

options.text: Nothing happens; sodium reacts only with water
options.rationale: Restricts the reaction to water because that is where sodium is usually met.

options.text: It fizzes and carbon dioxide gas is released
options.rationale: Borrows the gas from the reaction of an acid with a carbonate.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol burns completely in air. What are the products?

options.text: Carbon monoxide and water
options.rationale: Gives the products of incomplete combustion when the question specifies complete burning.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen
options.rationale: Assumes the hydrogen atoms leave as hydrogen gas rather than as water.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.rationale: Complete combustion of an alcohol gives carbon dioxide and water.

options.text: Ethanoic acid and steam
options.rationale: Confuses burning with oxidation by an oxidising agent, which does give ethanoic acid.

mcqs.stem: Which equation correctly represents the complete combustion of ethanol?

options.text: C₂H₅OH + 2O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: Carbon and oxygen both balance, at 2 C and 5 O each side, but the hydrogen does not: 6 on the left and only 2 on the right.

options.text: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: Written straight from the reactants and products without balancing at all.

options.text: C₂H₅OH + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 3H₂O
options.rationale: Balanced: two carbon atoms, six hydrogen atoms and seven oxygen atoms on each side.

options.text: C₂H₅OH + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O
options.rationale: The unbalanced word-to-symbol translation, with one of every product molecule.

mcqs.stem: What happens when ethanol is added to water?

options.text: It dissolves and the solution has a pH below 7
options.rationale: Assumes an –OH containing molecule must make the water acidic.

options.text: It floats as a layer and does not mix at all
options.rationale: Treats every organic liquid as immiscible with water, as an oil would be.

options.text: It dissolves fully, giving a neutral solution
options.rationale: The first four alcohols dissolve in water and their solutions have a neutral pH.

options.text: It reacts and hydrogen gas is given off
options.rationale: Carries the sodium reaction across to a mixture where no metal is present.

mcqs.stem: Ethanol is warmed with an oxidising agent. What is formed?

options.text: Ethene, formed by the loss of a water molecule
options.rationale: Confuses oxidation with dehydration, which removes water and gives an alkene.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water, as when it burns
options.rationale: Treats any reaction with oxygen present as full combustion.

options.text: Ethanoic acid, which is a carboxylic acid
options.rationale: Oxidation of an alcohol produces the carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms.

options.text: Ethyl ethanoate, an ester of the alcohol
options.rationale: Jumps to the ester, which needs an alcohol and an acid together, not an oxidising agent.

mcqs.stem: Which statement gives main uses of the first four alcohols?

options.text: They are used as fuels and as solvents
options.rationale: The specification requires recall of the main uses of these alcohols: as fuels and as solvents.

options.text: They are used only for alcoholic drinks
options.rationale: Takes the everyday meaning of alcohol as the whole of the chemistry.

options.text: They are used as fuels but never as solvents
options.rationale: Half remembered: fuels are recalled but the use as solvents is denied.

options.text: They are used mainly to neutralise acids
options.rationale: Follows from thinking the –OH group makes alcohols alkaline.

mcqs.stem: How are aqueous solutions of ethanol produced from sugar?

options.text: The sugar solution is fermented using yeast
options.rationale: The specification states that aqueous solutions of ethanol are produced when sugar solutions are fermented using yeast.

options.text: The sugar solution is distilled with a catalyst
options.rationale: Confuses the separation step that follows with the reaction that makes the ethanol.

options.text: The sugar is reacted with steam and a catalyst
options.rationale: Borrows the industrial hydration of ethene, which starts from an alkene and not from sugar.

options.text: The sugar solution is warmed with an acid
options.rationale: Assumes ethanol is made by an oxidation rather than by the action of yeast.

mcqs.stem: Which conditions are used for the fermentation of sugar using yeast?

options.text: About 100 °C, in solution, with air kept out
options.rationale: Assumes a higher temperature always speeds a reaction up, ignoring that heat kills the yeast.

options.text: About 30 °C, in solution, with air kept out
options.rationale: Fermentation needs yeast, an aqueous sugar solution, a warm temperature of roughly 30 °C and anaerobic conditions.

options.text: About 30 °C, in solution, with air bubbled in
options.rationale: Adds oxygen because respiration is remembered as needing air.

options.text: About 300 °C and high pressure, with a catalyst
options.rationale: The conditions for hydrating ethene, recalled in place of the fermentation conditions.

mcqs.stem: Which of these formulae is that of an alcohol?

options.text: CH₃COOH
options.rationale: Contains O and H together, so it is misread as an alcohol; the –COOH group makes it an acid.

options.text: C₃H₆
options.rationale: A hydrocarbon with no oxygen at all, chosen when alcohols are thought of as hydrocarbons.

options.text: CH₃COOCH₂CH₃
options.rationale: An ester; it contains the atoms of an alcohol but they are joined into an ester link.

options.text: CH₃CH₂OH
options.rationale: The –OH functional group at the end of the chain makes this an alcohol, ethanol.

mcqs.stem: Which functional group do carboxylic acids contain?

options.text: The carboxyl group, –COOH
options.rationale: The specification gives the functional group of the carboxylic acids as -COOH.

options.text: The hydroxyl group, –OH
options.rationale: The alcohol group; picked because –COOH does contain an O–H, so the two look alike.

options.text: A carbon–carbon double bond
options.rationale: The alkene group, chosen when functional groups are matched to families at random.

options.text: The ester group, –COO–
options.rationale: The link found in an ester, which is the product of an acid and an alcohol, not the acid itself.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives the first four members of the homologous series of carboxylic acids?

options.text: Ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic, pentanoic acid
options.rationale: Starts the series at two carbon atoms and adds a fifth member to make up the four.

options.text: Methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic and butanoic acid
options.rationale: These are the four carboxylic acids named in the specification.

options.text: Methanol, ethanol, propanol and butanol
options.rationale: The alcohols; chosen when the -ol and -oic acid endings are not held apart.

options.text: Methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, pentanoic acid
options.rationale: Leaves butanoic acid out of a series that runs one carbon atom at a time.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid can be represented as CH₃COOH. What does this form show?

options.text: An –OH group on a chain of two carbons
options.rationale: Picks out the O–H and stops there, which would make ethanoic acid an alcohol.

options.text: A –COOH group joined to a CH₃ group
options.rationale: Writing it this way separates the carboxyl group from the rest of the molecule.

options.text: Every bond of the acid, drawn out
options.rationale: Confuses this written form with a fully displayed formula.

options.text: Just the atom count, like C₂H₄O₂
options.rationale: Treats it as a molecular formula, which would lose the grouping it shows.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid is added to sodium carbonate. What happens?

options.text: It fizzes gently and hydrogen gas is given off
options.rationale: Takes the gas from the reaction of an acid with a metal instead of with a carbonate.

options.text: There is no reaction, since it is only a weak acid
options.rationale: Reads 'weak' as 'unable to react' rather than as partly ionised.

options.text: A white precipitate forms and the mixture clouds
options.rationale: Expects an insoluble solid because the organic acid is assumed not to dissolve.

options.text: It fizzes and carbon dioxide gas is given off
options.rationale: Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to release carbon dioxide, as other acids do.

mcqs.stem: What happens when ethanoic acid dissolves in water?

options.text: An acidic solution forms, with a pH below 7
options.rationale: Carboxylic acids dissolve in water to give acidic solutions.

options.text: A neutral solution forms, as with ethanol
options.rationale: Carries the behaviour of an alcohol in water across to an acid.

options.text: It does not dissolve, being an organic liquid
options.rationale: Assumes organic compounds are always immiscible with water.

options.text: An alkaline solution forms, from the –OH
options.rationale: Reads the O–H in the carboxyl group as making the solution alkaline.

mcqs.stem: Ethanoic acid is warmed with ethanol and an acid catalyst. What is formed?

options.text: Ethyl ethanoate, an ester, together with water
options.rationale: A carboxylic acid reacts with an alcohol to produce an ester; here the ester is ethyl ethanoate.

options.text: A salt and water only, as in neutralisation
options.rationale: Treats the alcohol as though it were an alkali, so the reaction is read as neutralisation.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water, as with a carbonate
options.rationale: Applies the carbonate reaction to a reagent that contains no carbonate.

options.text: Sodium ethanoate and some hydrogen gas
options.rationale: Brings in sodium from the reaction of alcohols with the metal, which is not present here.

mcqs.stem: Why is ethanoic acid described as a weak acid?

options.text: All of its molecules ionise in aqueous solution
options.rationale: Describes a strong acid; students often assume every acid ionises fully.

options.text: Only some of its molecules ionise in solution
options.rationale: A weak acid is only partially ionised in aqueous solution.

options.text: Its solutions are dilute rather than concentrated
options.rationale: Confuses the strength of an acid with the concentration of the solution.

options.text: It holds fewer hydrogen atoms than a strong acid
options.rationale: Counts hydrogen atoms in the formula instead of considering ionisation.

mcqs.stem: Solutions of hydrochloric acid and ethanoic acid have the same concentration. How do their pH values compare?

options.text: Ethanoic acid has the lower pH of the two
options.rationale: Assumes the organic acid must be the more strongly acidic of the pair.

options.text: Both have the same pH, as both are acids
options.rationale: Follows from thinking that equal concentrations always give equal pH values.

options.text: Ethanoic acid has a pH of more than 7
options.rationale: Confuses a higher pH with an alkaline one; a weak acid is still acidic.

options.text: Ethanoic acid has the higher pH of the two
options.rationale: It ionises only partially, so its solution has a lower concentration of H+ ions and a higher pH.

mcqs.stem: Which of these formulae is that of a carboxylic acid?

options.text: CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
options.rationale: An alcohol; the –OH is there but not the carbonyl that completes a carboxyl group.

options.text: CH₃CH₂OH
options.rationale: Ethanol, chosen when any oxygen-containing organic molecule is read as an acid.

options.text: C₃H₆
options.rationale: A hydrocarbon with no oxygen, so it cannot contain a carboxyl group.

options.text: CH₃CH₂COOH
options.rationale: The –COOH group at the end of the chain makes this propanoic acid.
